principles.text: A gap up into declining 9/21 EMAs and prior resistance after a big rally is not healthy action — those levels are where to focus short entries.
A strong Russell/IWM weekly historically lowers the odds of a >15% correction in SPY/QQQ — but treat it as reference only, never as a standalone reason to buy or sell.
Cap same-sector exposure: even if a setup is good, skip it when you already hold multiple positions in that sector on the same side.

The first pullback (long) or first bounce (short) into the 50 EMA after a breakdown/character change is a high-quality entry, especially in a stock that previously respected its moving averages closely.
Be willing to take a few tries at a high-conviction level with tight stops until the stock proves the thesis wrong.
Pre-compute position size before the open: shares = (account risk %, e.g. 3%) / (stop distance %). ~1% stop -> ~3x risk in position value, 1.5% stop -> ~2x; wider than 1.5% -> size down further.
Place the stop order immediately after the entry fills — never sit in a position without a working stop.
Use market orders (not stop-limits) for stop losses so the exit is guaranteed to fill when the stop price is hit.
Overnight gap risk is part of the game and roughly symmetric; a wider stop does not reduce the chance of a close landing near your stop, so don't widen stops to 'avoid' gaps.
Prefer shorting the stock itself over inverse/leveraged ETFs: the ETFs are less liquid, a volatile underlying doesn't need leverage, and every ETF forces you to track a second chart.
You don't have to be net bullish or bearish to be profitable — there is more than one correct play; in a polarized tape being in the right stock matters more than the directional call.
Review charts manually across sectors: the act of filtering hundreds of charts is itself how you read relative strength/weakness and the general market.

Let where the market opens relative to key levels (declining EMAs, unfilled gaps, AVWAP) decide timing: if the open favors your bias, take entries in the first 15-30 minutes; if it opens flat/weak against your bias, wait for the bounce into those levels.

Leverage doesn't change per-trade risk when risk is defined by tight stops; it lets you hold many small-risk positions at once (e.g. >10 at ~25% average size) and finance new trades with open profits when the market is paying.

The weekly/daily chart is the thesis and the lower time frames are only execution — take intraday entries only in the direction that aligns with the higher-time-frame read, and return to the big picture when time frames conflict.

Anchor entries to daily levels (9/21/50 EMA) with all the clues lining up — theme strength/weakness, relative strength, distribution candles (big red bars, long upper wicks) — rather than a single intraday candle pattern; exact intraday trigger can stay discretionary once the daily context is right.
New traders should be more systematic about entry rules — it reduces overtrading and makes it clear whether an entry is solid.
Treat shorts as short swings of a few days (shorter holds than longs) outside of true bear markets — but beware covering into ordinary strength too early.

In choppy markets, mostly sit in cash but keep working: study relative strength across sectors and run imaginary trades (where to enter, whether a scary bounce should stop you) so you don't panic-cover or panic-sell when holding real positions.
